newsitem.title: INDIA: India takes wait-and-see stance toward UK's Labour.
newsitem.headline: India takes wait-and-see stance toward UK's Labour.

text.p: India said on Monday that it disagreed with the longstanding views of Britain's Labour party on the divided region of Kashmir but still hoped bilateral relations would improve under Prime Minister Tony Blair.
"On Kashmir, we have agreed to differ," a Foreign Ministry spokesman told reporters in the Indian capital. "However, we should wait for Labour in government to articulate its views."
Indian officials have privately expressed fears over the Labour party's stance on Kashmir.
Before winning Britain's election last week, Blair was quoted by Indian media as saying his government would seek to help negotiate an accord on Kashmir between India and Pakistan.

The Labour leader told a regional Indian newspaper during the election campaign that Britain, as the former imperial power in India, must accept its responsibility in a dispute stretching back 50 years.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947, two of them over Kashmir. Labour was in power in Britain when the subcontinent was partitioned.

India says the issue can be discussed only bilaterally with Pakistan, without the involvement of a third party. Pakistan wants an internationally supervised referendum of Kashmiris and says outside help would be welcome to help resolve the dispute.
Police and hospitals say more than 20,000 people have been killed in the Himalayan state of Jammu and Kashmir since 1990 when simmering discontent with Indian rule erupted into an armed rebellion.
The chief of Jammu and Kashmir on Monday urged Britain's new government to ignore Kashmiri separatists' pleas and not meddle in the half-century-old regional conflict.
Jammu and Kashmir chief minister Farooq Abdullah said he hoped Blair would concentrate on solving his nation's own "problems", including strife in Northern Ireland, and not interfere in Kashmir.
"I think now time has come when India and Pakistan should heal their own wounds without interference from any other country of the world," Abdullah told a news conference.
Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral is set to hold talks with his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif, in the Maldives on May 12 ahead of a regional summit.
The Foreign Ministry spokesman said New Delhi was waiting to see if the Labour government would adopt a pragmatic approach towards India which would promote economic ties.

"We note new Labour is broadly business friendly and values economic relations," the spokesman said. "Hence we are very optimistic we will continue to have the same or even greater levels of relations."

Indian officials said they believed Blair's large margin of victory would diminish the chances of his bowing to members of parliament representing constituencies with large numbers of Pakistani emigrants.
